how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← EV charger installation bid calculator

How much should I charge to install an EV charger?

Homeowners search that question and get back a single number. It hides the two things that actually set the price: how far the circuit has to run, and whether the panel has room for it. A 20–25 foot indoor Level 2 install on a spare breaker slot is one job. The same 48 A charger on a 70-foot trench to a detached garage that also needs a service upgrade is several times the price — and neither is what a flat "EV charger install" quote is pricing.

Open the free EV charger bid calculator

What a flat hang fee cannot see

Breaker sizing. EVSE is a continuous load, so the overcurrent device is sized at 125% of the charger's continuous current and rounded up to a standard breaker — 32 A becomes 40 A, 48 A becomes 60 A. That changes the wire gauge, not just a line item.

The run. Copper has to hold voltage drop over the actual distance, not a nameplate distance. A 25-foot indoor run and a 70-foot outdoor run to a detached structure are different conductor sizes and different labor hours, even at the same amperage.

The trench. Anything outside the structure the panel is on means trenching, conduit, and backfill — hours a "charger install" line item does not carry.

Panel capacity. Subtract a realistic existing load from the service rating. If what's left is smaller than the EVSE breaker, the job needs a service upgrade or a load-management device, not an optimistic assumption that the panel has room.

A bid you can defend

  1. Confirm the charger's continuous amperage and size the breaker at 125%.
  2. Measure the actual run and pick copper that holds voltage drop over that distance, not a nameplate distance.
  3. Add trench and backfill hours if the run leaves the structure the panel is on.
  4. Check remaining service capacity; price a service upgrade or load management if there isn't room.
  5. Load the wage (payroll burden), then add permit and overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin).

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It is not a permit load calculation and does not determine NEC or local-code compliance — confirm the panel, the run, and the adopted code with a licensed electrician before you bid.

Worked example

A 48 A charger on a spare panel slot, 25 feet indoors, needs a 60 A breaker and a short, inexpensive run — call it close to a thousand dollars of contractor price once wage burden, permit, and margin are in. The same 48 A charger on a 70-foot trench to a detached garage, where the service also needs an upgrade to clear the new breaker, is several times that number before either job has been marked up. The calculator prices both from the same inputs so a "how much for an EV charger" phone quote never has to guess which job it is.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install an EV charger?

There is no flat hang fee. A 20–25 foot indoor Level 2 install on a panel with a spare slot often lands near a thousand dollars of contractor price once wage burden, permit, and margin are in. The same 48 A charger on a 70-foot trench to a detached garage that also needs a service upgrade is several times that. Price the circuit, the run, the trench, and the panel work.

What size breaker does a Level 2 EV charger need?

EVSE is a continuous load. Size the overcurrent device at 125% of the charger's continuous current and round up to a standard breaker: 32 A → 40 A, 40 A → 50 A, 48 A → 60 A, 80 A → 100 A. Confirm against the charger nameplate and the adopted code in the jurisdiction.

When does an EV charger install need a service upgrade?

When the existing service does not have enough unused capacity for the new breaker. Subtract a realistic existing load from the service rating. If the remainder is smaller than the EVSE breaker, the bid should include a service upgrade or a load-management device — not a hope that the panel will be fine.

No warranty. This free page is not electrical, engineering, code, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a panel is safe. It is not a permit load calculation and it does not determine NEC or local-code compliance. Verify every figure against your own takeoff, the nameplate, the adopted code, and a licensed electrician before relying on it or submitting a bid. FOR ELECTRICAL CONTRACTORS

Bid the run and the panel, not the charger.

A Level 2 EVSE is a continuous load. Size the breaker at 125%, pick copper that holds a 3% voltage drop for the actual run, then add trench hours and panel work. A 25-foot indoor hang on a spare slot is one job. The same 48 A charger on a 70-foot trench to a detached garage that also needs a service upgrade is several times that price — and a flat “EV charger install” quote cannot see the difference.

How much should I charge to install an EV charger? · hardwire or a NEMA 14-50 outlet? · this calculator vs. a flat hang fee · vs. ServiceTitan · vs. Workiz

The job

Starting figures are common takeoff points, not a code opinion. Replace every length and hour with what you measured on this house.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation (high in electrical), liability, and paid time off. Pricing off the raw journeyman rate is the most common reason a charger hang that looked profitable was not.

Questions electricians actually type

How much should I charge to install an EV charger?

There is no flat hang fee. Use this page: a short indoor 48 A job on a spare slot often lands near $1,200–$1,400 at the default rates. Switch the location to a detached garage, add a 60-foot trench, and pick a service upgrade — the same charger becomes a several-thousand-dollar job. That gap is the whole product.

What size breaker and wire does a 48 A charger need?

48 A continuous × 1.25 = 60 A breaker. Copper #6 usually carries that ampacity; a long run may upsize to hold 3% voltage drop at 240 V. The result panel shows the gauge and the calculated drop for the feet you entered.

Do I have to include a service upgrade?

Only if the existing service does not have the headroom. Enter the service rating and a honest existing-load estimate. If the new breaker is larger than the unused capacity, the tool flags it — it does not decide the upgrade for you, and it is not a permit load calculation. A 200 A service already estimated at 190 A of existing load has only 10 A of headroom; a 48 A charger needs a 60 A breaker, so that job gets flagged even though the panel itself has a free slot.

Why does a long run sometimes need thicker wire than the breaker alone requires?

Ampacity and voltage drop are two different limits. A 48 A charger's 60 A breaker is carried by #6 copper on ampacity alone, but at 160 feet that #6 run would sit past the 3% voltage-drop budget at 240 V. The calculator checks both and upsizes to #4 (1.98% drop at 160 ft) whenever the shorter-run wire would fail the drop check — the wire size shown is whichever limit binds for the feet you entered, not just the breaker size.

How much can a detached garage and a service upgrade add to the price?

At the default rates, a 48 A indoor hang on a spare slot with a 25-foot run prices near $1,263. Move the same charger to a detached garage with a 70-foot run, a 60-foot trench, and a service upgrade, and it prices near $4,587 — largely trench labor and restoration, the extra outdoor labor rate, and the 8 hours a service upgrade adds to the panel line. Same charger, almost 3.6× the price, because the job is not the charger.

What does the baseline comparison number mean?

The result panel prices your entered job against a fixed reference — the same wage, burden, overhead, and margin, but a 48 A indoor hang, 20-foot run, spare panel slot, no trench, no hardware. At the defaults that baseline prices near $1,189, so a $1,263 quote reads as about 6% over it. That reference is the "easy garage" number a customer often has in mind from a flat-fee ad; the ratio shows how far your actual job's numbers move it, not whether either price is right.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

should-i-hardwire-or-use-a-nema-14-50.ht.text:
← EV charger installation bid calculator

Should I hardwire the EV charger or install a NEMA 14-50 outlet?

Both connect the same circuit to the same charger, so the decision is not really about price -- the calculator prices the two only about a hundred dollars apart on a typical install. It is about whether the homeowner wants to unplug the EVSE, and about which connection type the charger's own manufacturer warranties.

Open the free EV charger bid calculator

What actually differs

Hardwired. The circuit conductors land directly on the EVSE's terminal block or junction box -- no plug, no receptacle. There is one fewer connection in the circuit, and it is not the connection type most exposed to a continuous full-amperage load for hours at a time.

NEMA 14-50 receptacle. The EVSE plugs in like a range or an RV. That buys portability -- unplug it to swap chargers, take it when you move, or share the circuit with an RV or welder that also uses a 14-50 -- at the cost of one more connection that has to be rated and installed for continuous duty, not just for the occasional high draw a 14-50 was originally used for.

Manufacturer warranty. Read the EVSE's installation manual before deciding. Some chargers ship as hardwired-only, some as plug-in-only, and some support both but only warranty one -- this is a real constraint from the manufacturer, not a code question this page can answer.

Worked example

Same 48 A charger, same 25-foot indoor run, same spare panel slot, same wage and margin settings -- installed both ways, priced by this calculator's own bid engine:

Install typeLabor hoursContractor price
Hardwired EVSE5.65$1,263.36
NEMA 14-50 receptacle6.05$1,374.04

The receptacle version runs $110.67 higher -- a $45 listed 14-50 device plus about 24 extra minutes to mount and terminate it, both marked up through the same overhead and margin as the rest of the job. That gap holds roughly steady across runs and locations; it is not the number that should decide this, since a longer run or a trench moves the total by far more than $111 either way.

Common questions

Should I hardwire an EV charger or install a NEMA 14-50 outlet?

Hardwiring lands the EVSE's conductors directly on a junction box with no plug or receptacle in the circuit, which removes the one connection in the circuit rated for continuous duty that is a plug-and-receptacle pair rather than a fixed splice. A NEMA 14-50 receptacle costs a little more in parts and labor but lets the homeowner unplug the EVSE -- to swap chargers, sell the house without leaving hardware behind, or share the circuit with an RV or welder that also uses a 14-50 plug. Check the charger manufacturer's installation manual first: several EVSE models only warranty one connection type.

Is a NEMA 14-50 receptacle install more expensive than hardwiring?

Only slightly. On a typical 48 A install this calculator prices the receptacle version about $111 higher than hardwired, all else equal -- the device itself plus roughly 24 extra minutes of labor to mount and terminate it. That gap is much smaller than what location, run length, or panel work move the price by, so it should not be the deciding factor on its own.

Does a NEMA 14-50 need to be a special continuous-duty receptacle?

Use a receptacle and plug listed for the charger's continuous load -- EVSE draws its full rated current for hours at a time, which is harder on contact quality than the intermittent draw a standard 14-50 was originally rated for. Confirm the specific device the manufacturer's installation manual calls for and the adopted code in the jurisdiction; this page does not make that determination for you.

Can I switch from a plug-in charger to hardwired later?

Usually, if the run and breaker were already sized for it -- the receptacle gets removed and the conductors land directly on the EVSE's terminal block, which is a smaller job than the original install. Going the other direction (hardwired to plug-in) means adding a receptacle and a compatible EVSE, which is closer to redoing the termination end of the job. Either direction is a real labor item, not a five-minute swap, and should be bid as one.

No warranty. vs-a-flat-hang-fee.html.text:
← EV Charger Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat hang fee

"$1,200 to install an EV charger" is not a price for a job — it is a price for whatever circuit the fee happened to be built on, quietly applied to every driveway that also asks for a Level 2 charger.

What a flat hang fee is

A flat hang fee is the fastest way to quote a charger install over the phone: ask the charger's amperage, quote a number, skip the walkthrough. Homeowners shop it because a search result or a Facebook ad already gave them a number, and it is the number they will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually a short indoor or attached-garage run to a panel with a spare breaker slot and plenty of service headroom — and then reused for every driveway afterward, whether or not the next one needs a trench, a longer run, or a panel that is already full.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the charger's continuous amps, the install type, the one-way run and any trench footage, the mounting location, the panel work, and the existing service amps and estimated existing load, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, permit fee, and target margin. It sizes the breaker at 125% of the continuous load, recommends copper that holds a 3% voltage drop over the actual run, flags a panel with no headroom for the new circuit, and returns the bid price, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this run and this panel, not a flat number for every driveway.

What a flat hang fee doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee for a 25-foot indoor hang and a 70-foot trench to a detached garage — even though the trench job alone can need a full day more of labor. Prices the run and any trench footage separately, at minutes per foot for the run and hours plus restoration dollars per foot for the trench.
Has no line for a service upgrade, a subpanel, or a relocate, regardless of whether the existing panel has headroom for the new breaker. Sizes the required breaker at 125% of the charger's continuous amps and flags when the existing service has no headroom for it, before you commit to a price.
Quotes the same copper for a 20-foot run and a 150-foot run, with no check against voltage drop. Recommends the smallest copper conductor that carries the breaker and holds a 3% voltage-drop budget over the actual run, upsizing automatically on long pulls.
Has no separate line for an outdoor disconnect, a driveway pedestal, or a NEMA 14-50 receptacle instead of a hardwired unit. Prices outdoor disconnects, pedestal hardware, and receptacle devices as their own material and labor lines when the job calls for them.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat hang fee would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two driveways, one flat fee

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

A 25-foot indoor hardwired hang for a 48 A charger, on a spare breaker slot with headroom on the existing 200 A service, prices at $1,263.36, on a job that costs $947.52 to run.

Take the same 48 A charger to a detached garage instead — a 70-foot run through a 60-foot trench, with a panel that also needs a 200 A service upgrade — and the job costs $3,439.95 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator bids it at $4,586.61: 3.6 times the easy job, on the identical charger. Quoting the trench-and-upgrade job at the easy job's flat $1,263.36 fee prices it $2,176.59 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $3,323.25 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at a 25% target margin. Same charger, same flat fee, one driveway that pays and one that loses money the moment the trench is dug.

Common questions

Why does a flat hang fee get an EV charger install wrong?

Because the cost driver is the circuit, not the charger. A 25-foot indoor run to a panel with a spare breaker slot needs a short copper pull and about half an hour of panel work. A 70-foot trench to a detached garage that also needs a 200 A service upgrade needs a full day of trench and panel labor, restoration, and a much larger material bill, on the same charger. A flat hang fee charges both the same because it was priced on the charger, not the circuit.

What does a flat hang fee usually leave out entirely?

The run, the trench, and the panel. A flat fee has no line for a 125%-continuous-load breaker sized off the charger's actual amps, no line for copper upsized to hold a 3% voltage drop over a long run, no line for trench footage or restoration, and no line for panel work heavier than a spare slot -- a relocate, a subpanel, or a full service upgrade.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: a 25-foot indoor hardwired hang for a 48 A charger, on a spare breaker slot with headroom on the existing 200 A service, prices at $1,263.36. The same 48 A charger over a 70-foot run through a 60-foot trench to a detached garage that also needs a 200 A service upgrade prices at $4,586.61 -- 3.6 times the easy job. Quoting the trench-and-upgrade job at the easy job's $1,263.36 flat fee prices it $2,176.59 below its own $3,439.95 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit or the crew's time is covered.

Is a flat hang fee ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- an indoor or attached-garage run to a panel with a spare slot and headroom on the service -- a flat fee can land close, because that is probably the job the fee was set on. The risk is quoting a detached-garage trench or a tight panel the same way sight unseen, because the fee does not know the run length, the trench, or the panel's headroom until someone measures the house, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's copper and breaker pricing, or your permit fees. It takes the charger amps, the run, the trench footage, the mounting location, the panel work, and the existing service and load, plus your own wage, burden, overhead, permit, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat hang fee skips, not a market survey.

Open the EV Charger Install Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read how much you should charge to install an EV charger.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a permit load calculation and does not determine NEC or local-code compliance. Verify every figure against your own takeoff, wage, and material costs, and against a licensed electrician, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running an electrical company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one EV charger install cost, given its amps, its run, and its panel situation, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves electrical, HVAC, plumbing, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving the electrical trade among others, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule electricians, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's charger continuous amps and install type (hardwired or a NEMA 14-50 receptacle), the mounting location (indoor garage, outdoor wall, detached garage, or pedestal), the one-way run and any trench footage, the panel work the job needs (a spare slot through a service upgrade), and the existing service and estimated existing load, plus journeyman wage, payroll burden, permit and inspection fee, charger hardware where it is not owner-supplied, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into the price, the labor hours behind it, the effective hourly rate, the price per circuit amp and per run foot, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that floor. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Workiz?

They do different jobs, and an electrical contractor of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Workiz is a field service management platform used by electrical, HVAC, and other trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, payments, and reporting across a business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from the continuous amps of the charger and the install type, with the one-way run, trench footage, mounting location, panel work, and the existing service and load as their own line items, plus journeyman wage, payroll burden, permit, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the price, the labor hours behind it, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. An electrical contractor who already schedules electricians, dispatches crews, and invoices across every job is better served by Workiz or a comparable field service platform; a shop that wants an instant, private answer to what one EV charger install should cost from its amps, its run, and its panel situation is in the right place here.

Does this calculator size the wire and breaker for me?

It shows a suggested breaker size, a wire recommendation, and the voltage drop over the run you entered, because those three change the cost of the job more than anything else on the form and a bid written without them is a guess. They are an estimating aid and nothing more. This page is not a permit load calculation, it does not determine NEC or local-code compliance, and it does not tell you a panel is safe. Verify every figure against your own takeoff, the nameplate, the adopted code, and a licensed electrician before you submit a bid or pull a permit.
